rationale: A wins because it knows when to stop: "Instacart Built Its Brand on Grocery Delivery. Its Advertising Business Just Hit $1 Billion." gives the founder a defensible revenue-mix story without pretending the stock market has already mispriced anything. B has sharper raw instincts, especially "The checkout line is disappearing in a few hundred grocery stores. What happens to the people who staffed it?", but it also leads with "whether investors are pricing an ads company or a delivery company" and then claims the angle needs no outside proof. That is how a good idea walks into fact-check trouble.
gaps_in_A: "a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" overstates the update; the facts say Instacart has 1,500 retail banners and plans to expand smart carts, not that carts are planned across all banners.
"as digital attribution has gotten harder" is industry wallpaper not in the update. Prove it or cut it.

"What 6,000 Consumer Brands Buying Grocery Ads Reveals About Where CPG Money Is Moving" is too close to "Instacart Has Become a Retail Media Network"; the buyer-side version needs a named advertiser or spend-shift proof to stand alone.
It misses the obvious skeptical read on checkout-skipping carts: labor impact. A founder needs that question before a workplace or retail-labor reporter asks it first.
gaps_in_B: "More than 6,000 brands now buy grocery ads from a company that does not own a store" uses a hook not supplied in the update. It may be true, but this exercise gave facts, not permission to freelance.
"whether investors are pricing an ads company or a delivery company" is a capital-markets frame with no stock price, analyst view, valuation multiple, or revenue mix.
"The checkout line is disappearing" overstates the smart-cart fact; the carts let shoppers skip checkout in a few hundred stores, not erase checkout lines.
"needs no outside proof beyond the numbers you already hold" contradicts its own proof list, which asks for ad share, order-growth period, and run-rate methodology.
